title: The Bloody Palette of the Animal Kingdom
content:
_[This story](https://knowablemagazine.org/content/article/living-world/2026/why-animal-blood-comes-in-different-colors) was originally published by_[Knowable Magazine](https://knowablemagazine.org/content/article/society/2026/prehistory-lost-threads)_._

Whether it’s gushing from a bumped nose or pooling atop a pricked finger, our blood is some hue of red. But red-bloodedness isn’t universal in the animal kingdom. In some creatures, the vital fluid is purple, in others it’s yellow, green or even white.

What imparts these different colors to the liquid of life? To find out, _Knowable_ _Magazine_ waded into the research and spoke with a couple of scientists who have studied the stuff: John Postlethwait, a developmental geneticist at the University of Oregon, and Zachary Cheviron, an ecophysiologist at the University of Montana. Here’s what’s known about the science behind the hues.

**Bizarre Blues and Purples**

The rich red of vertebrate blood comes from hemoglobin, a protein in red blood cells that contains iron atoms. Hemoglobin’s job is to deliver oxygen, and its iron atoms, which grab onto oxygen, make our blood look red. When iron atoms are attached to oxygen, blood is a bright cherry red; when less oxygen is bound it’s a muddier brown-red. But many creatures don’t use hemoglobin. Octopus and squid, for example, and crustaceans such as shrimp and crabs, rely on [a protein called hemocyanin](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40925714/) to ferry oxygen around. Hemocyanin has copper atoms — which look blue when bound to oxygen — instead of hemoglobin’s iron.

Hemocyanin doesn’t bind to oxygen as efficiently as hemoglobin does. But it functions especially well in cold temperatures, such as those found in the deep ocean. And it can have more jobs than carrying oxygen in the creatures that use it — research suggests that hemocyanins can play an immunity role, aiding in healing wounds, for example.

Horseshoe crabs (left) bleed blue, thanks to copper-rich hemocyanin, while icefish (right) don’t use an oxygen-carrying protein and bleed ghostly white. _Credit: Recherches Sur L’Anatomie des Limules 1873 (left); Antarctic Fishes of the Scottish National Antarctic Expedition 1913 (right)_

Other marine creatures, such as clam-like brachiopods and the seafloor dwelling peanut worm, bleed violet — but not because of hemocyanin. Instead, these creatures use an iron-rich, purple-colored protein [pigment called hemerythrin](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5363010/) to shuttle oxygen throughout their blood.

**Chilling Chartreuse**

Some sea squirts — squishy, potato-shaped ocean-living animals — bleed greenish yellow. They do not produce hemoglobin, and there’s some debate about what imparts the yellowish hue. One candidate is the element vanadium, which many sea squirts concentrate in their blood.

Another theory points to diet. When sea squirts metabolize their staple meal, marine phytoplankton, they create carotenoids, pigments that are yellow, red or orange.

Different mechanisms can make animals bleed full-on green. Several lizard species in New Guinea use hemoglobin to transport oxygen around, like vertebrates typically do. But then they break down the hemoglobin into a naturally green pigment called biliverdin (the same molecule, when present in high concentrations, causes the yellow-green appearance of jaundice in people). And unlike most vertebrates that metabolize biliverdin into other, duller compounds, these New Guinea lizards [accumulate the pigment in their blood](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.aao5017) to the point that its green hue overwhelms the red of hemoglobin in the bloodstream and tissues.

**Creepy and Clear**

Antarctic blackfin icefish of the family Channichthyidae are the only known vertebrates that don’t make hemoglobin and do not have red blood cells. Their blood is a milky, translucent white. “They really are kind of ghostly,” says Postlethwait.

Instead of hemoglobin or any equivalent oxygen-binding protein, the icefish rely on oxygen dissolving directly into their bloodstream. They also have larger hearts and capillaries compared with other Antarctic fish, and these can pump and circulate greater quantities of blood. Icefish are patient ambush predators — they lie in wait rather than darting around to catch their meals, expending less energy and requiring less oxygen use.

A recent study of icefish by Postlethwait and colleagues investigated the genomes of several fish species to understand why genes for making hemoglobin have been deleted from the creatures’ DNA. Whether icefish first lost their red blood cells and then their hemoglobin, or vice versa, is still a mystery, Postlethwait says. What drove the loss is also a puzzle. One notion the researchers suggest is that the cold waters of Antarctica’s Southern Ocean were oxygen-rich enough to render the middle-man job of hemoglobin obsolete.

**Supercharged Hemoglobin**

The bizarre colors that blood can take on are just the start of what’s amazing about blood. And the findings keep coming. In high-altitude ecosystems, many species must [cope with low oxygen](https://knowablemagazine.org/content/article/health-disease/2025/overcoming-risks-of-pregnancy-at-high-elevation). This has pushed the hemoglobin of some mountain dwellers into overdrive.

The deer mouse, for example, can live up to 14,000 feet above sea level — thousands of feet higher than the point that many humans start to develop altitude sickness. The mouse has evolved hemoglobin that [makes extra tight bonds with oxygen](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0905224106). [](https://knowablemagazine.org/content/article/living-world/2024/how-hummingbirds-adapt-to-an-extreme-lifestyle)[Andean hummingbirds](https://knowablemagazine.org/content/article/living-world/2024/how-hummingbirds-adapt-to-an-extreme-lifestyle) and high-altitude [black-spotted frogs](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/ecology-and-evolution/articles/10.3389/fevo.2023.1103406/full) have [similar alterations](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1315456110) to their hemoglobin, too.

Yet there are always tradeoffs with adaptations, says Cheviron of the University of Montana. That high-elevation deer mouse, for example, has some trouble getting oxygen off the hemoglobin and into its tissues. They make up for missed oxygen deliveries, he says, by having higher quantities of oxygen-releasing mitochondria in their muscle fibers.

The more scientists look, the more they uncover exquisite variations of this type within blood: cells “remarkably tuned by evolution,” says Postlethwait, “that facilitate the wonderful diversity of life-forms that inhabit our Earth.”

Weird blood across the animal kingdom can also inform human health. Hemoglobin evolution in the tiny deer mouse could inspire therapies for hypoxia-inducing diseases, Cheviron says, including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. And for the nearly 2 billion people living with anemia, or insufficient red blood cells or hemoglobin, the transparent bleeders of the Antarctic may hold clues to new treatments. “Clearly,” says Postlethwait, “the icefish have figured it out.” ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: This Dark Spot on the Moon Might Be a Giant Lunar Cave
content:
You’ve heard of the dark side of the moon, but NASA is also looking to explore a dark _spot_ on the moon that it thinks may be a giant underground cave system.

An image of the spot, known as the Marius Hills Pit (MHP), was snapped by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO). Based on initial estimates, it’s thought that the hole could be nearly 300 feet wide and about 150 feet deep.

This is the Marius Hills Pit, but we’re not exactly sure what’s underneath it. _Credit: NASA/GSFC/Arizona State University_

But it’s what this hole might lead to that really interests experts. The thinking is that the pit could be an entrance to a subterranean network of caves and lava tubes, created by lava flows on the moon from billions of years ago.

Not only does that make the MHP of great interest geologically, it also means it could provide valuable shelter against the radiation and extreme temperatures that astronauts are otherwise exposed to on the moon. In other words, it could make for a prime lunar base location.

The long-term aim is to return astronauts to the lunar surface. _Credit: NASA_

Earlier this month, NASA decided to go ahead with an investigation of the MHP proposed by the Planetary Science Institute. The mission is going to be called the Geophysical Instruments for Marius Lunar Pit Investigation, or GIMLI, and it will combine a payload of seismic sensors, ground-penetrating radar, and a gravimeter (for measuring gravitational fields) to detect what’s underneath the pit.

Delivered by an as-yet-unspecified lander, the GIMLI equipment will still prove useful even if there isn’t a cave or lava tube network connected to the MHP. The readings the instruments take should give researchers more clues about how the pit originally formed, providing us additional information about the ancient history of our planet’s nearest neighbor.

“Confirming a substantial lava tube would give us an insight into how volcanism operated on the moon,” Gareth Morgan, the Deputy Principal Investigator on the GIMLI program said in a [statement](https://www.psi.edu/blog/psi-led-team-selected-for-nasa-prism-program/). “Lava tubes are a common feature of basaltic volcanism on Earth, so identifying them on the moon means we could use knowledge of such terrestrial caves to better understand lunar history.”

Two other payloads for a future lander have also [just been selected](https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-adds-new-science-investigations-for-moon-base/) by NASA: the Lunar Environment Monitoring Station – South Pole instrument suite for monitoring the lunar environment and any potential hazards, and the Depth Imager with Spectral and Color Optics for detecting ice on the surface of the moon.

All of these projects have been designed to lay the foundations for the return of humans to the moon. So perhaps one day, astronauts won’t just be calling this dark spot on the moon Marius Hills Pit, they’ll also be calling it home. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: How Voting Is Like a Klein Bottle
content:
A new topological model connects a centuries-old voting paradox to a surface with no distinct inside or outside.

Mathematically speaking, democracy is next to impossible.

That may sound like the premise of a Silicon Valley billionaire’s six-hour podcast, but it’s actually a statement about a remarkably stubborn problem: How do you translate a group of individual preferences into a single choice?

In 1785, the French mathematician and philosopher [Nicolas de Condorcet (opens a new tab)](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Marie-Jean-Antoine-Nicolas-de-Caritat-marquis-de-Condorcet) discovered that a majority can sometimes vote itself into a logical loop. In elections with three or more candidates, each voter might rank the candidates in a perfectly clear and consistent way — yet when all the votes are tallied, every candidate loses in a head-to-head contest against one of their rivals. Changing the rules only gets us so far: As the economist Kenneth Arrow later proved, any method for combining individual rankings into a collective order must sacrifice at least one seemingly reasonable democratic requirement.

Now three researchers have shown that Condorcet’s 240-year-old paradox [has a shape (opens a new tab)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.07283), and it’s suitably peculiar: a Klein bottle, a surface with no distinct inside or outside. The result gives mathematicians a geometric way to explore why seemingly reasonable rules for collective decision-making can become impossible to reconcile.

## **Everyone Loses to Someone**

When there are only two choices, the will of the people is easy to divine: Barring a tie, the candidate preferred by a majority wins. Add a third contender, however, and things get weird. Suddenly, even agreeing on what it means to win becomes a problem.

You might simply elect whoever receives the most votes, as in a typical American election. But suppose Alice receives 35% of the vote, Bob 34%, and Carol 31%. Alice wins. Yet if Carol’s supporters all prefer Bob to Alice, then 65% of the electorate would rather have Bob. By one perfectly reasonable definition of majority rule, the wrong candidate has won.

Before anyone reaches for a tinfoil hat, let’s be clear: Every ballot is counted correctly. The question is what should count as winning.

One solution is to ask voters to rank the candidates, then choose whoever would defeat every rival in a head-to-head contest. But consider the following scenario:

*   One-third of voters rank Alice over Bob over Carol.
*   One-third rank Bob over Carol over Alice.
*   One-third rank Carol over Alice over Bob.

Now compare the candidates in pairs:

*   Alice beats Bob, because the first and third groups prefer Alice to Bob.
*   Bob beats Carol, because the first and second groups prefer Bob to Carol.
*   Carol beats Alice, because the second and third groups prefer Carol to Alice.

Every voter has a perfectly coherent ranking, yet together they have produced a result that runs in circles.

This is the paradox that Condorcet, a passionate believer in democracy, encountered in the late 18th century. As the secretary of the French Academy of Sciences, he’d been looking for ways to make sure the group was choosing new members fairly. (More enlightened than most, Condorcet would also question the democratic arithmetic of excluding half the population, explicitly defending women’s political rights in a 1790 essay. A few years later, during the Reign of Terror, the revolution he had supported put him in a prison cell; he was found dead two days after his arrest.)

Over the centuries, mathematicians, political scientists, and reformers have devised an astonishing variety of voting systems in hopes of breaking Condorcet’s impasse. Yet every method brings its own vulnerabilities. Change the system and you may well change the winner, even when the voters and their preferences remain exactly the same.

In 1951, the economist Kenneth Arrow showed how deep the problem ran. He sought a voting system that stayed consistent while meeting just a few simple democratic requirements. Voters should be free to rank the candidates in any order. No single voter should unilaterally dictate the outcome of an election. (Read: no kings.) If everyone prefers one option to another, the group’s ranking should reflect that preference. And the ranking of two candidates should depend only on how voters compare those two: Where voters place Carol on their ballots shouldn’t affect whether the group ranks Alice above Bob.

Each requirement sounds reasonable enough on its own. But, Arrow showed, no method can satisfy them all. “Quite often the will of the people doesn’t exist,” said [Iain McLean (opens a new tab)](https://www.politics.ox.ac.uk/person/iain-mclean) of the University of Oxford.

[Arrow’s impossibility theorem (opens a new tab)](https://www.jstor.org/stable/j.ctt1nqb90), as this result is now known, extended Condorcet’s paradox beyond majority rule, establishing a fundamental limit on how individual votes can be combined into a group decision.Different voting systems can change which of Arrow’s requirements fail, but no single system can ever preserve them all. “You have to make a choice as a system designer as to which of the conditions it’s most harmless to fail,” McLean said.

In 1980, to better understand this phenomenon, the mathematician and economist [Graciela Chichilnisky (opens a new tab)](https://econ.columbia.edu/econpeople/graciela-chichilnisky/)[turned to topology (opens a new tab)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0001870880900328), an area of math in which shapes are considered equivalent if one can be stretched into another without tearing. In a footnote, she mused that Condorcet’s paradox in particular could be thought about as a topological problem.

Now mathematicians have proved her intuition true.

## **The Shape of a Paradox**

What, then, does a voting paradox _look_ like?

To answer this question, the new work builds on a model that [Yuliy Baryshnikov (opens a new tab)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0196885883710201), now a professor at the University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign, proposed in 1993. First, consider a single voter’s ballot in an election with three candidates. There are six possible ways to rank the options. Each one can be represented by a triangle:

Each corner of this triangle represents one of the comparisons the ballot implies: Alice over Bob, Bob over Carol, and Alice over Carol.

A different ballot listing Alice first, Carol second, and Bob third agrees on two of those comparisons, since both ballots put Alice above her rivals. Their triangles therefore share two corners and can be joined along the edge connecting them.

Now join all six triangles (representing all possible ballots) along their matching edges. You get a strip:

The edges at its two ends also match. So bend the strip around and glue those edges together, matching the labels. You get a tube with an opening at each end:

Baryshnikov used this model to give a new topological proof of Arrow’s impossibility theorem.

But look at what happens at either end of the tube. Around one rim, the comparisons read Alice over Bob, Bob over Carol, and Carol over Alice. Around the other, the cycle runs in reverse.

We’re left with Condorcet’s paradoxical cycles — voting results that run in circles. Baryshnikov had ignored these rims. But 30 years later, in April 2025, [Ori Livson (opens a new tab)](https://www.ori-livson.com/), a doctoral student at the University of Sydney, reconsidered them. After all, sometimes such circular relationships are allowed, as in the rules of [rock-paper-scissors (opens a new tab)](https://www.rpsgame.org/). The trouble arises in situations like elections, when those relationships are expected to form a consistent ranking. Livson wanted a topological model that could distinguish cases where the cycles are allowed from cases where they aren’t.

Together with his adviser, [Mikhail Prokopenko (opens a new tab)](https://profiles.sydney.edu.au/mikhail.prokopenko), and Prokopenko’s longtime colleague [Siddharth Pritam (opens a new tab)](https://siddharthpritam.com/) of the Chennai Mathematical Institute, he set out to model the troublesome case.

Each cycle around the tube’s rims leads to the same impossible conclusion: Every candidate ranks above every other. In that sense, both rims are saying the same thing. And in topology, “once you realize two things are the same, you can glue them together,” Livson said.

So how should you join the rims?

If you bend the tube until its two openings meet, you get a doughnut-shaped surface called a torus. But this gluing also connects individual edges from each rim in pairings that represent incompatible relationships. An edge representing “Bob over Alice over Carol,” for instance, gets glued to an edge representing “Bob over Carol over Alice.” The researchers needed a way to join the rims without creating such contradictions.

The solution? A twist. Instead of matching one rim to the other point by point, in the same order, the twist allowed the researchers to reverse the order of preferences around one of the rims — making the cycles equivalent. “Gluing with the twist is the only valid option,” Livson said.

If you twist a strip of paper and join its edges, you get a surface with only one side, called a Möbius strip. But what happens when you twist a tube? You end up with something remarkable and strange: a Klein bottle.

Like a Möbius strip, a Klein bottle has only one side, with no distinct inside or outside. Unlike a Möbius strip, it has no edge. (If it looks as if this surface crosses itself, it does — in three dimensions. Mathematicians avoid this by constructing the Klein bottle in four dimensions, where it can close up without self-intersecting.)

The trio had their model. Just as each voter can supply a coherent ranking, and yet the electorate’s preferences refuse to fit into a single order, each small patch of a Klein bottle appears to have two sides, yet those sides cannot be distinguished consistently across the whole surface. In both cases, something that makes sense piece by piece breaks down when we try to put the pieces together.

For Livson, Pritam, and Prokopenko, that resemblance raises a larger question: Can topology help explain other fundamental limits on what mathematics can accomplish? Perhaps these different impossibilities, when given a shape, will turn out to share a deeper geometric explanation.

So where does that leave democracy?

Topology makes the paradox tangible, but choosing a voting system still means picking your poison. Mathematics can tell us what the trade-offs entail. Our priorities determine which ones are worth making. And that’s something no theorem can settle for us. “It’s not really a mathematical debate,” McLean said. “It’s a debate about values.”

# 20 Favorite Children’s Books from 20 Years of The Marginalian

### By Maria Popova

“Anyone who writes down to children is simply wasting his time,” E.B. White [insisted](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/02/26/e-b-white-writing-for-children/). “You have to write up, not down. Children are demanding. They are the most attentive, curious, eager, observant, sensitive, quick, and generally congenial readers on earth.”

Both as a reader of them and as [a writer of them](http://themarginalian.org/books), I have never considered “children’s books” a separate category of literature: The best children’s books are works of philosophy in disguise, shining a sidewise gleam on the fundamental questions we live with, articulating in the language of children, which is the language of great simplicity and great profundity, the most complex truths about being human. title: The Dark Wood of the Golden Birds: Margaret Wise Brown’s Lost Masterpiece about Mortality and the Meaning of Life, Newly Illustrated
content:
[![Image 1: The Dark Wood of the Golden Birds: Margaret Wise Brown’s Lost Masterpiece about Mortality and the Meaning of Life, Newly Illustrated](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/darkwood_ofraamit_cover.jpg?fit=320%2C516&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Dark-Wood-Golden-Birds/dp/1961341638/?tag=braipick-20)

In early September 1948, a year after she rewilded the landscape of literature with _Goodnight Moon_, [Margaret Wise Brown](https://www.themarginalian.org/tag/margaret-wise-brown/) watched [the love of her life](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/08/28/margaret-wise-brown-michael-strange-poems/) fade to black.

Michael Strange, born Blanche Oelrichs, had cast an instant spell on Margaret — outspoken, sophisticated, and self-possessed, so tall Margaret had to lift her grey-blue eyes to meet the black of Michael’s, her tall frame clad in masculine clothing she herself had designed to cling to her curves, with a musical voice unspooling from her haunting dark beauty, a deep velvet laugh, and a reputation for rarely keeping a promise. In her tight tweed pants and long-tailed blazers and oversized ties, she moved effortlessly through the sea of gloves and lace and whispering society ladies.

When her wealthy family of Austrian royal lineage had found her erotic poetry embarrassing, Blanche had emancipated herself under the male nom de plume, which soon became a stage name as she strode into the theater world as playwright and actress, and eventually swelled into a total persona — the name with which she signed her letters, the name by which her intimates addressed her, the name of her self-image.

![Image 2](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/michaelstrange_margaretwisebrown.jpg?resize=680%2C513&ssl=1)

Michael Strange and Margaret Wise Brown

In her youth, Blanche had been named the most beautiful woman in Paris. Now, about to turn fifty-eight, Michael Strange was a ghost on a New York stage, her skin sallow, her body emaciated to the size of a child’s after refusing to let her aggressive leukemia keep her from performing.

Margaret and Michael had met seven years earlier. One day on Vinalhaven — the Maine island where Margaret would spend much of her life and write most of her books — she had rowed to a lover’s cottage and found the luscious stranger sunbathing there with her lover. Soon, back in New York, she was surprised to receive a lunch invitation from Michael, who had shown up dressed in fur from head to toe, asking bold questions about her love life while sipping sherry. Margaret was thirty, Michael fifty and on her third unhappy marriage; her latest husband had never read her poetry. Both women were born in the wrong century, bent on bending it to their will; both were accidental radicals, just by living unselfconsciously; both had had affairs with Thomas Wolfe; both were at heart poets more than anything else.

By the middle of the World War, they were lovers; Michael had declared that she had never loved anyone the way she loved Margaret and never would; she had promised to love her until her dying day.

Late one night, Margaret’s phone rang. Michael’s voice poured in, sped up with alarm, imploring her to get into a taxi right away. Her husband had found out about their relationship and, in an era when the diagnostic manual of psychiatry classified same-sex love as a mental illness, was threatening to have her locked away in an asylum. A doctor was on his way to “diagnose” her. With her maid’s help, Michael managed to slip out through the back staircase and into the taxi as Margaret was pulling up.

On the disorienting ride through the New York nocturne, they weighed their options and decided to head to the high-society women’s club Michael frequented. There, she collected herself, phoned her husband to demand a formal apology, then set the wheels in motion for a legal separation.

From this point on, Michael became — to use the modern term, hard-won and ahistorical — Margaret’s partner. Soon, they were living across the hallway from each other, in a pair of twin apartments on the East End, with Margaret part nominal tenant and part unnamed wife as she was quickly becoming one of the country’s most original and beloved children’s book authors.

It was a stormy love that pushed and pulled, but grafted itself onto Margaret’s being. Michael wrote adoring letters and criticized Margaret’s diction at dinner parties. She gave her a golden wishbone necklace and a ring, made her feel like she was too needy, and derided her children’s books as unsophisticated, “silly furry stories,” not Real Literature: an actress and socialite who had not published a poem in a decade and was feeling abandoned by her own muse, deriding one of the most vibrantly creative people of the past century — poet, songwriter, progressive education reformer, author of more than a hundred singularly wondrous books for the young, with which she would earn herself a little red house, a yellow convertible, and the love of millions of children; the author whom the visionary [Ursula Nordstrom](https://www.themarginalian.org/tag/ursula-nordstrom/) had no qualms calling her favorite author, despite also publishing Maurice Sendak, Shel Silverstein, and E.B. White. Even Michael’s pet name for Margaret was laced with this ambivalent mixture of affection and disdain: Bunny-no-good.

And yet nobody ever knows what electrifies the infinite sky between two people, what magnetizes them together, what roils deep beneath the faint surface trails left in letters and diaries and the recollections of bystanders, what animates the long days between the islanded moments crashed by emotion and frozen in time. Margaret loved Michael with unassailable devotion, and Michael was dying. So she did the hardest thing in life — facing the death of a beloved while remaining a pillar for their passage — the best way she knew how: She wrote a love letter in the form of a children’s book.

[![Image 3](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/darkwood_ofraamit1.jpg?resize=680%2C1124&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Dark-Wood-Golden-Birds/dp/1961341638/?tag=braipick-20)

Art by Ofra Amit for [_The Dark Wood of the Golden Birds_](https://www.amazon.com/Dark-Wood-Golden-Birds/dp/1961341638/?tag=braipick-20).

[![Image 4](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/darkwood_ofraamit3.jpg?resize=680%2C1117&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Dark-Wood-Golden-Birds/dp/1961341638/?tag=braipick-20)

Art by Ofra Amit for [_The Dark Wood of the Golden Birds_](https://www.amazon.com/Dark-Wood-Golden-Birds/dp/1961341638/?tag=braipick-20).

On the last day of spring in 1950, three years after _Goodnight Moon_ had enraptured the world with its bright playfulness, [**_The Dark Wood of the Golden Birds_**](https://www.amazon.com/Dark-Wood-Golden-Birds/dp/1961341638/?tag=braipick-20), somber and numinous with its elegiac prose, and its haunting duotone of otherworldly greens and yellows, and its simple dedication: “For Michael Strange.”

Margaret asked her longtime collaborator Leonard Weisgard — one of the most prolific and beloved picture-book artists of the century — to illustrate it. She urged him to do it as fast as possible in order to rush the book to the printer and press it into Michael’s hands while she was still alive. He agreed out of love for Margaret, but he resented being rushed and did not condone her relationship with Michael. For an artist of such staggering talent and versatility, the [unfeeling two-tone illustrations](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/09/30/the-dark-wood-of-the-golden-birds-margaret-wise-brown/) he produced for this layered, lovely book were by far his weakest. They didn’t help the book’s fate, already up against a culture that has no room and no language for grief, and no tolerance for the darkest dimensions of life, which crack open our vastest capacity for light — it fell out of print.

I learned about _The Dark Wood of the Golden Birds_ through a footnote in a volume of Ursula Nordstrom’s letters. Had I not just lost a beloved friend, I might not have gone on the long dusty search for a surviving copy. When I finally found one, I fell instantly under the spell of this crepuscular story aglow with love and longing. It was odd to see such unfeeling illustrations for something so deeply felt. When [Marginalian Editions](https://www.themarginalian.org/editions/) was born of the conviction that the best way to complain is to create, I invited the wildly talented [Ofra Amit](https://www.ofra-amit.com/) — who had illustrated my book [_The Universe in Verse_](https://www.themarginalian.org/uiv-book/) — to reimagine Margaret’s love letter to the mystery of death in a [new edition](https://www.amazon.com/Dark-Wood-Golden-Birds/dp/1961341638/?tag=braipick-20) that does justice to the subtlety, strangeness, and splendor of the story, bittersweet and beautiful like the transience of life itself.

[![Image 5](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/darkwood_ofraamit_endpapers.jpg?resize=680%2C558&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Dark-Wood-Golden-Birds/dp/1961341638/?tag=braipick-20)

# 20 Favorite Books from 20 Years of The Marginalian

### By Maria Popova

It is a beautiful dream, that there is something out there to instruct you how to live — a secret handed down by your parents or your teachers, a system like liberal arts education or cognitive behavioral therapy, a slogan held up by your heroes declaring the answer to the bottomless question of why you are here.

Whenever you wake up, however you wake up, you find yourself on a path no one else can walk for you, a path you must make by walking. Still, you can find signposts that keep you from losing your way in loneliness. “You think your pain and your heartbreak are unprecedented in the history of the world,” James Baldwin [wrote](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/05/24/james-baldwin-life-magazine-1963/), “but then you read.”

In [celebrating twenty years of _The Marginalian_](https://www.youtube.com/live/qKd8UMjQ2Mo) — this ongoing record of learning how to live written in marginalia on the books I have read — I have attempted the impossible: to distill a lifetime of reading into the twenty books that have served as the most enduring signposts, apart from [those I have written](https://themarginalian.org/books) (which always both shape and are shaped by a writer’s life more profoundly than any books read). title: The Baloney Detection Kit: Carl Sagan’s Timeless Tenets of Critical Thinking
content:
[![Image 1](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/06/demonhauntedworld_sagan.jpg?w=680&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/The-Demon-Haunted-World-Science-Candle/dp/0345409469/?tag=braipick-20)**Carl Sagan** (November 9, 1934–December 20, 1996) was many things — a [cosmic sage](https://www.themarginalian.org/2012/12/10/pale-blue-dot-motion-graphics/), [voracious reader](https://www.themarginalian.org/2012/07/11/carl-sagan-reading-list/), [hopeless romantic](https://www.themarginalian.org/2011/12/27/the-voyagers-penny-lane-carl-sagan/), and [brilliant philosopher](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/12/20/carl-sagan-varieties-of-scientific-experience/). But above all, he endures as our era’s greatest patron saint of reason and critical thinking, a master of [the vital balance between skepticism and openness](https://www.themarginalian.org/2012/05/23/carl-sagan-the-burden-of-skepticism/). In [**_The Demon-Haunted World: Science as a Candle in the Dark_**](https://www.amazon.com/The-Demon-Haunted-World-Science-Candle/dp/0345409469/?tag=braipick-20) ([_public library_](http://www.worldcat.org/title/demon-haunted-world-science-as-a-candle-in-the-dark/oclc/32855551&referer=brief_results)) — the same indispensable volume that gave us Sagan’s timeless meditation on [science and spirituality](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/06/12/carl-sagan-on-science-and-spirituality/), published mere months before his death in 1996 — Sagan shares his secret to upholding the rites of reason, even in the face of society’s most shameless untruths and outrageous propaganda.

In a chapter titled **“The Fine Art of Baloney Detection,”** Sagan reflects on the many types of deception to which we’re susceptible — from psychics to religious zealotry to paid product endorsements by scientists, which he held in especially low regard, noting that they “betray contempt for the intelligence of their customers” and “introduce an insidious corruption of popular attitudes about scientific objectivity.” (Cue in [PBS’s Joe Hanson on how to read science news](http://explore.noodle.org/post/70511854124/so-great-so-necessary-joe-hanson-of-its-okay).) But rather than preaching from the ivory tower of self-righteousness, Sagan approaches the subject from the most vulnerable of places — having just lost both of his parents, he reflects on the all too human allure of promises of supernatural reunions in the afterlife, reminding us that falling for such fictions doesn’t make us stupid or bad people, but simply means that we need to equip ourselves with the right tools against them.

[![Image 2](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/11/carlsagan1.jpg?w=680&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/The-Demon-Haunted-World-Science-Candle/dp/0345409469/?tag=braipick-20)

Through their training, scientists are equipped with what Sagan calls a “baloney detection kit” — a set of cognitive tools and techniques that fortify the mind against penetration by falsehoods:

> The kit is brought out as a matter of course whenever new ideas are offered for consideration. If the new idea survives examination by the tools in our kit, we grant it warm, although tentative, acceptance. If you’re so inclined, if you don’t want to buy baloney even when it’s reassuring to do so, there are precautions that can be taken; there’s a tried-and-true, consumer-tested method.

But the kit, Sagan argues, isn’t merely a tool of science — rather, it contains invaluable tools of healthy skepticism that apply just as elegantly, and just as necessarily, to everyday life. By adopting the kit, we can all shield ourselves against clueless guile and deliberate manipulation. Sagan shares nine of these tools:

> 1.   Wherever possible there must be independent confirmation of the “facts.”
> 2.   Encourage substantive debate on the evidence by knowledgeable proponents of all points of view.
> 3.   Arguments from authority carry little weight — “authorities” have made mistakes in the past. They will do so again in the future. Perhaps a better way to say it is that in science there are no authorities; at most, there are experts.
> 4.   Spin more than one hypothesis. If there’s something to be explained, think of all the different ways in which it could be explained. Then think of tests by which you might systematically disprove each of the alternatives. What survives, the hypothesis that resists disproof in this Darwinian selection among “multiple working hypotheses,” has a much better chance of being the right answer than if you had simply run with the first idea that caught your fancy.
> 5.   Try not to get overly attached to a hypothesis just because it’s yours. It’s only a way station in the pursuit of knowledge. Ask yourself why you like the idea. Compare it fairly with the alternatives. See if you can find reasons for rejecting it. If you don’t, others will.
> 6.   Quantify. If whatever it is you’re explaining has some measure, some numerical quantity attached to it, you’ll be much better able to discriminate among competing hypotheses. What is vague and qualitative is open to many explanations. Of course there are truths to be sought in the many qualitative issues we are obliged to confront, but finding _them_ is more challenging.
> 7.   If there’s a chain of argument, _every_ link in the chain must work (including the premise) — not just most of them.
> 8.   Occam’s Razor. This convenient rule-of-thumb urges us when faced with two hypotheses that explain the data _equally well_ to choose the simpler.
> 9.   Always ask whether the hypothesis can be, at least in principle, falsified. Propositions that are untestable, unfalsifiable are not worth much. Consider the grand idea that our Universe and everything in it is just an elementary particle — an electron, say — in a much bigger Cosmos. But if we can never acquire information from outside our Universe, is not the idea incapable of disproof? You must be able to check assertions out. Inveterate skeptics must be given the chance to follow your reasoning, to duplicate your experiments and see if they get the same result.

[![Image 3](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/01/carlsagan.jpg?w=680&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/The-Demon-Haunted-World-Science-Candle/dp/0345409469/?tag=braipick-20)

Just as important as learning these helpful tools, however, is unlearning and avoiding the most common pitfalls of common sense. Reminding us of where society is most vulnerable to those, Sagan writes:

> In addition to teaching us what to do when evaluating a claim to knowledge, any good baloney detection kit must also teach us what not to do. It helps us recognize the most common and perilous fallacies of logic and rhetoric. Many good examples can be found in religion and politics, because their practitioners are so often obliged to justify two contradictory propositions.

He admonishes against the twenty most common and perilous ones — many rooted in our [chronic discomfort with ambiguity](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/11/11/dani-shapiro-still-writing-2/) — with examples of each in action:

> 1.   **_ad hominem_** — Latin for “to the man,” attacking the arguer and not the argument (e.g., _The Reverend Dr. Smith is a known Biblical fundamentalist, so her objections to evolution need not be taken seriously_)
> 2.   **argument from authority** (e.g., _President Richard Nixon should be re-elected because he has a secret plan to end the war in Southeast Asia_ — but because it was secret, there was no way for the electorate to evaluate it on its merits; the argument amounted to trusting him because he was President: a mistake, as it turned out)
> 3.   **argument from adverse consequences** (e.g., _A God meting out punishment and reward must exist, because if He didn’t, society would be much more lawless and dangerous_ — perhaps even ungovernable. Or: _The defendant in a widely publicized murder trial must be found guilty; otherwise, it will be an encouragement for other men to murder their wives_)
> 4.   **appeal to ignorance** — the claim that whatever has not been proved false must be true, and vice versa (e.g., _There is no compelling evidence that UFOs are not visiting the Earth; therefore UFOs exist — and there is intelligent life elsewhere in the Universe._ Or: _There may be seventy kazillion other worlds, but not one is known to have the moral advancement of the Earth, so we’re still central to the Universe._) This impatience with ambiguity can be criticized in the phrase: absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.
> 5.   **special pleading**, often to rescue a proposition in deep rhetorical trouble (e.g., _How can a merciful God condemn future generations to torment because, against orders, one woman induced one man to eat an apple? Special plead: you don’t understand the subtle Doctrine of Free Will_. Or: _How can there be an equally godlike Father, Son, and Holy Ghost in the same Person? Special plead: You don’t understand the Divine Mystery of the Trinity._ Or: _How could God permit the followers of Judaism, Christianity, and Islam — each in their own way enjoined to heroic measures of loving kindness and compassion — to have perpetrated so much cruelty for so long? Special plead: You don’t understand Free Will again. And anyway, God moves in mysterious ways._)
> 6.   **begging the question**, also called **assuming the answer** (e.g., _We must institute the death penalty to discourage violent crime. But does the violent crime rate in fact fall when the death penalty is imposed?_ Or: _The stock market fell yesterday because of a technical adjustment and profit-taking by investors_ — but is there any independent evidence for the causal role of “adjustment” and profit-taking; have we learned anything at all from this purported explanation?)
> 7.   **observational selection**, also called **the enumeration of favorable circumstances**, or as the philosopher Francis Bacon described it, counting the hits and forgetting the misses (e.g., _A state boasts of the Presidents it has produced, but is silent on its serial killers_)
> 8.   **statistics of small numbers** — a close relative of observational selection (e.g., _“They say 1 out of every 5 people is Chinese. How is this possible? I know hundreds of people, and none of them is Chinese. Yours truly.”_ Or: _“I’ve thrown three sevens in a row. Tonight I can’t lose.”_)
> 9.   **misunderstanding of the nature of statistics** (e.g., _President Dwight Eisenhower expressing astonishment and alarm on discovering that fully half of all Americans have below average intelligence)_;
> 10.   **inconsistency** (e.g., _Prudently plan for the worst of which a potential military adversary is capable, but thriftily ignore scientific projections on environmental dangers because they’re not “proved.”_ Or: _Attribute the declining life expectancy in the former Soviet Union to the failures of communism many years ago, but never attribute the high infant mortality rate in the United States (now highest of the major industrial nations) to the failures of capitalism._ Or: _Consider it reasonable for the Universe to continue to exist forever into the future, but judge absurd the possibility that it has infinite duration into the past)_;
> 11.   **_non sequitur_** — Latin for “It doesn’t follow” (e.g., _Our nation will prevail because God is great. But nearly every nation pretends this to be true; the German formulation was “Gott mit uns”_). Often those falling into the non sequitur fallacy have simply failed to recognize alternative possibilities;
> 12.   **_post hoc, ergo propter hoc_** — Latin for “It happened after, so it was caused by” (e.g., _Jaime Cardinal Sin, Archbishop of Manila: “I know of … a 26-year-old who looks 60 because she takes [contraceptive] pills.”_ Or: _Before women got the vote, there were no nuclear weapons_)
> 13.   **meaningless question** (e.g., _What happens when an irresistible force meets an immovable object? But if there is such a thing as an irresistible force there can be no immovable objects, and vice versa_)
> 14.   **excluded middle**, or **false dichotomy** — considering only the two extremes in a continuum of intermediate possibilities (e.g., _“Sure, take his side; my husband’s perfect; I’m always wrong.” Or: “Either you love your country or you hate it.” Or: “If you’re not part of the solution, you’re part of the problem”_)
> 15.   **short-term vs. long-term** — a subset of the excluded middle, but so important I’ve pulled it out for special attention (e.g., _We can’t afford programs to feed malnourished children and educate pre-school kids. We need to urgently deal with crime on the streets._ Or: _Why explore space or pursue fundamental science when we have so huge a budget deficit?)_;
> 16.   **slippery slope**, related to excluded middle (e.g., _If we allow abortion in the first weeks of pregnancy, it will be impossible to prevent the killing of a full-term infant_. Or, conversely: _If the state prohibits abortion even in the ninth month, it will soon be telling us what to do with our bodies around the time of conception)_;
> 17.   **confusion of correlation and causation** (e.g., _A survey shows that more college graduates are homosexual than those with lesser education; therefore education makes people gay._ Or: _Andean earthquakes are correlated with closest approaches of the planet Uranus; therefore — despite the absence of any such correlation for the nearer, more massive planet Jupiter — the latter causes the former_)
> 18.   **straw man** — caricaturing a position to make it easier to attack (e.g., _Scientists suppose that living things simply fell together by chance_ — a formulation that willfully ignores the central Darwinian insight, that Nature ratchets up by saving what works and discarding what doesn’t. Or — this is also a short-term/long-term fallacy — _environmentalists care more for snail darters and spotted owls than they do for people_)
> 19.   **suppressed evidence**, or **half-truths** (e.g., _An amazingly accurate and widely quoted “prophecy” of the assassination attempt on President Reagan is shown on television_; but — an important detail — was it recorded before or after the event? Or: _These government abuses demand revolution, even if you can’t make an omelette without breaking some eggs._ Yes, but is this likely to be a revolution in which far more people are killed than under the previous regime? What does the experience of other revolutions suggest? Are all revolutions against oppressive regimes desirable and in the interests of the people?)
> 20.   **weasel words** (e.g., The separation of powers of the U.S. Constitution specifies that the United States may not conduct a war without a declaration by Congress. On the other hand, Presidents are given control of foreign policy and the conduct of wars, which are potentially powerful tools for getting themselves re-elected. Presidents of either political party may therefore be tempted to arrange wars while waving the flag and calling the wars something else — “police actions,” “armed incursions,” “protective reaction strikes,” “pacification,” “safeguarding American interests,” and a wide variety of “operations,” such as “Operation Just Cause.” Euphemisms for war are one of a broad class of reinventions of language for political purposes. Talleyrand said, “An important art of politicians is to find new names for institutions which under old names have become odious to the public”)

Sagan ends the chapter with a necessary disclaimer:

> Like all tools, the baloney detection kit can be misused, applied out of context, or even employed as a rote alternative to thinking. But applied judiciously, it can make all the difference in the world — not least in evaluating our own arguments before we present them to others.

[**_The Demon-Haunted World_**](https://www.amazon.com/The-Demon-Haunted-World-Science-Candle/dp/0345409469/?tag=braipick-20) is a timelessly fantastic read in its entirety, timelier than ever in a great many ways amidst our present media landscape of propaganda, pseudoscience, and various commercial motives. Complement it with Sagan on [science and “God”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/12/20/carl-sagan-varieties-of-scientific-experience/).

![Image 1](http://dynomight.net/img/math/the-dance-lesson.jpg)![Image 2](http://dynomight.net/img/math/the-dance-lesson.jpg)![Image 3](http://dynomight.net/img/math/the-dance-lesson.jpg)![Image 4](http://dynomight.net/img/math/the-dance-lesson.jpg)![Image 5](http://dynomight.net/img/math/the-dance-lesson.jpg)

This is a weird moment. I have a hunch that we’ll look back later and tell ourselves stories in which it seemed obvious where things were going. So I wanted to lay down a little time capsule and register just how confusing everything felt at the time. This is a personal view from the trenches.

## 1.

If you’re a normal person, you may feel that AI has been good at math for a long time.[1](http://dynomight.net/math#fn:1) But for “real” math, this is roughly what it felt like:

| When | Feeling |
| --- | --- |
| 2024 | LLMs are toys |
| Summer 2025 | LLMs are interesting toys |
| Early Autumn 2025 | LLMs can do useful stuff sometimes |
| Mid Autumn 2025 | …a lot of stuff |
| Late Autumn 2025 | …a _lot_ |
| Early 2026 | holy god |

Even having been astonished by AI progress in the past, it was still astonishing to see AI move in a matter of months from a mildly-useful toy to something that many people now consider almost impossible to do without.

## 2.

Personally, I’d say that current AI makes me around 50% more productive at “doing math”. That’s despite the fact that AI can now often do in a few minutes things that would have taken me hours to do myself.

The main reason is that my concept of “doing math” involves various steps, like coming up with ideas for theorems, trying to prove them, writing things down, reorganizing everything to make it more clear, and so on. AI is good at some parts of this, but still pretty bad at others, so the overall speedup isn’t as high as you might expect.

(Even if planes could go 10× faster, your door-to-door travel time from your apartment in London to your friend’s place in Rome wouldn’t decrease _that_ much, because you still have to get to the airport and wait to board.)

## 3.

But then, I’m still (sort of; more on this later) trying to follow my old “doing math” workflow, just automating certain parts of it. That can’t be right, can it?

If we found a way to make batteries at 1% of the current cost, we wouldn’t just say, “cool, batteries are cheap now”. We’d find all sorts of new ways to use batteries that didn’t make sense before, and change the ways we generate power to account for all these new batteries. Probably our whole energy system would end up transformed. Analogously, AI being good at proofs should lead to a very different equilibrium. But what is that?[2](http://dynomight.net/math#fn:2)

## 4.

It seems healthy, at the moment, to maintain a fluid view of what “doing math” means. But at bare minimum it surely involves _understanding_ the math that “I” am “doing”. So long as that’s part of the workflow, it would seem to impose a limit on how quickly “I” could “do” math, no matter how good AI is.

One obvious conclusion would be that my tiny organic brain should be removed from the workflow entirely. Maybe! But it’s interesting to speculate about how much faster things could go while still keeping a human brain in the loop. I think the answer is: A lot.

## 5.

Contrary to what you may have heard, humans _are not_ obsolete for math. Not yet. The most obvious reason is that AI is still bad at writing.

People often complain that AI writing overuses various patterns or lacks a unique voice or whatever. I don’t disagree, but I always felt like there was a deeper issue that I couldn’t quite put my finger on. With math, this becomes very clear: The problem is it _doesn’t make any goddamned sense_.

Really, I think it’s deeper than being bad “at writing”. It seems like AI is bad at _thinking_ in certain ways that manifest as bad writing.

## 6.

When novices do math, they often create “spaghetti-code math”: Imagine a long document with lots of equations, but if you point at any one equation, it’s hard to say what assumptions underpin it, or how it fits into the bigger picture. Any random idea that was mentioned 17 pages ago might be used again at any time with no warning. With experience, people learn to break complex arguments down into modular pieces with a good “API”, in the sense that the assumptions and conclusions for each part are relatively simple.

Somehow, AI has developed these amazing technical skills, while still being bad at creating abstractions So the arguments it gives are long and tangled and bewildering. This is what makes AI math seem so alien.

## 7.

Now I know what you’re thinking. Maybe AI isn’t bad at creating abstractions. It’s just bad at creating abstractions that work _for you_, human with tiny organic brain.

From a distance, that seems plausible. And it might be true to some degree. I have high-bandwidth access to a human brain. It’s not crazy to imagine that this gives me an advantage in predicting how a human brain would react to a given presentation of ideas. But still, I claim that current AI is _objectively_ bad at creating abstractions, regardless of if the consumer of those abstractions is human or artificial.

Here’s why: If I ask AI to prove something hard, it will produce a proof that starts simple and gradually descends into a rampage of complexity. If I tell it to break that proof down into self-contained pieces, it will produce lemmas that each take a full page just to state. If I ask, “Why? Why have you done this to me?”, the AI will say, “This is as simple as it gets. It’s not that bad. What’s your problem?”

But if I argue with the AI for a while, I can start to understand the basic contours of the argument. And I’ll ask, “Why don’t you first just try to prove blah using only assumptions blahblah, without worrying about blahblahblah? Wouldn’t that be easier?” Often, this doesn’t work, either because my idea was bad, or because the AI isn’t smart enough to do it. (Which one? Who knows!) But after a few attempts, I can usually find something that that works, and the AI can use it to re-write the proof in a somewhat simpler way. If I repeat this many times, I can gradually chip away at the complexity.

But maybe that’s still just making the proof easier for humans to understand? No! For one, this usually makes the proof shorter, and sometimes dramatically shorter. More importantly, during this process, someone (maybe me, maybe the AI) will often realize that there’s a different proof strategy that gives a _stronger result_. Instead of proving `x < 9.7`, now we can prove `x < 7.1`. Thus, artisanal human abstractions are “objectively” useful.

## 8.

Some people might claim that it’s already possible to automate some of what I’m doing with some multi-agent Rube Goldberg thing. I’m not sure, because my experience has been that investing lots of time into clever `AGENTS.MD` or custom skills or harnesses isn’t a great use of time. That stuff _is_ somewhat helpful, but things are changing so fast that the knowledge has a short half-life. Also, the majority of information about these tricks seems to come from people who are excited about the technology itself.

On the other hand, [the automator](https://dynomight.net/automated/) told me to try typing, “ask independent agents for an adversarial review”, and I’ve found those seven words to be quite helpful. I wish I could find a source with boring best practices for people who are happy to stay away from the bleeding edge.

## 9.

Another reason AI doesn’t improve my productivity more is that it is often the green light, the orgastic future that [recedes before me](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Page:The_Great_Gatsby_-_Fitzgerald_-_1925.djvu/163). I’ll ask AI to do something, and it will _almost_ seem to do it. So I’ll ask for changes, and it seems to help, but it’s still not quite right. Hours later, I’ve accomplished nothing and learned nothing. Eventually, I start over, either doing it myself or with AI on a very tight leash, and I’m done in 30 minutes. Each time this happens I feel foolish and tell myself not to do it again. But it’s very hard to judge in real-time.

## 10.

Of course, I’m not claiming that AI is intrinsically bad at writing or thinking or abstraction-making. It’s gotten better at all of these and I expect it will continue to do so. All I’m saying is that as of Autumn 2026, humans still have a lot to contribute, and it’s not just better exposition.

## 11.

Did AI actually get much better at math in Autumn 2025? Or perhaps, in the grand scheme of things, human math ability falls into a narrow range?

## 12.

Some people are responding to the new reality by gleefully using AI to generate lots of semi-OK-ish papers and puking them up on [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/). I understand the incentives that drive this. In some sense, it seems like the logical response to the new reality. (After inventing cars, we started taking a lot more low-value trips.) But I don’t think this is socially useful, and I tend to think everyone will soon agree that this is embarrassing. But… I’m not sure. Maybe it is socially useful? And I find myself feeling vaguely jealous of the people who are wired this way, who instead of feeling blinkered, see opportunity and plunder.

## 13.

Want an optimistic pro-AI, pro-progress take? OK. If I take my old “doing math” workflow, AI makes it strictly better. A _lot_ better. It’s like having a hyper-conscientious intern that is smarter than me in many ways, works at incredible speed, and knows approximately everything.

Yes, AI sucks at writing and making abstractions. But if I’m disciplined and try to mostly do the math “myself” while asking the AI for help, I can explore ideas much faster than before, make far fewer mistakes, and produce something just as clear as before, while developing just as much understanding. I can ask, “What happens if you do a Kofuni expansion?”, and get an answer instantly. I can ask for illustrations or interactive visualizations and see them instantly. Arguably, we’re incredibly lucky to be alive at this moment, when these new tools have opened up this new territory to explore.

## 14.

And isn’t that what I wanted? Back in 2024, I [bemoaned](https://dynomight.net/automated/) that what AI most seemed to struggle with was getting the facts straight:

> Perhaps the old science fiction robots were a projection of our fantasies. I want my style and voice to be precious and uncopyable. I want an AI assistant that will tirelessly hunt down facts while I provide creativity and panache and magic. But that’s not how it is. So we should remember: In a scenario where AI is useful but humans retain some comparative advantage, we might not like where that comparative advantage lies.

At least with math, and at least for the moment, _I_ get to be Kirk, while the AI is Spock. (Even with other types of writing, my impression is that since 2024, AI has improved more along Spock dimensions than along Kirk dimensions.) So that’s nice.

## 15.

In the last few months, it frequently happens that a collaborator will use AI to generate something, and then send it to me and ask me to check if it’s useful. I can see why this seems reasonable. (Really, I do.) But when it happens a lot, one can’t help but wonder what the point of the human collaborator is.

## 16.

On the other hand—with creative writing, my advice is not to use AI to write, at all. Ask questions if you want, but write every damned word yourself.[3](http://dynomight.net/math#fn:3) With math, I don’t feel like such a hard line makes sense. It seems that creating something good still requires a _lot_ of human involvement, to the point of agonizing over notation, repeatedly re-organizing things, and heavily editing individual sentences. Still, I find that if people make that effort, they can create something just as good as they could by hand, while still being perhaps 50% AI written.[4](http://dynomight.net/math#fn:4)

So I don’t mind if people send me “centaur math”, provided they take responsibility for the contents. The problem is that when working with AI, it takes constant paranoid vigilance to avoid letting things slip beyond your understanding. I often find myself wanting to awkwardly ask people, “OK, you obviously used AI to make this… which is OK… but how much of this do you vouch for? If we have a meeting to discuss it, will you crumble the moment I start asking questions?”

## 17.

When I’m in abstraction-creation mode, I feel like I’m doing something intelligent. When yell at AI about bad notation and writing, I feel like I’m providing taste. But I often find myself giving feedback that seems incredibly basic. Things like: This is a mess, clean it up. Or: Do you need that assumption? Or: If you can’t solve this problem, why don’t you create a simpler version and try to solve it first?

On the one hand, I guess a lot of what good human managers do amounts to giving very basic feedback. On the other hand, it’s hard to imagine that I have much durable advantage in doing this kind of thing. So I wonder how much durable advantage I have in abstraction-making or taste, too.

## 18.

A common reaction to AI getting better at proofs is that humans need to focus more on exposition. This has an obvious [Bourdieu](https://dynomight.net/bourdieu/)-esque criticism: Human painters used to strongly value photo-realism, but after cameras were invented they convinced everyone that, oops, photo-realism isn’t important, what matters is _expression_, which coincidentally cameras can do. Isn’t a shift towards exposition in math just a way for humans to move the goalposts and justify their own continued relevance?

The only credible way I see to avoid that criticism seems to be to bite the bullet and say that, in fact, math should have _already_ have focused more on exposition, even before AI. Personally, I strongly believe that this is true.

## 19.

I think the biggest reason I’m not more productive is: What’s the point? In the past, if you came up with an elegant proof, you’d tell yourself, “I made a thing! Other people will read and use my thing! I am advancing human progress.” You can still tell yourself that now. But you have to wonder, will anyone actually read your proof? Or will they just ask another AI to explain it to them? Will your proof help their AI explain it better? For how long? If you just waited a year, would some other AI produce that same proof independently?
